gap: To reach D7's target, prove an aggregate restriction inequality for every unrestricted fan-in-2 B2 circuit computing MCSP[m^c], with arbitrary sharing and fan-out, strong enough to imply CC_B2(F_m) not in O(2^m m^k) for each fixed k. Per-restriction gate consumption alone does not control repeated use of shared gates.
proved_step:
statement: For m>=1 and a Boolean function f:{0,1}^m->{0,1} with t>=1 accepting inputs, a DNF using one minterm for each accepting input computes f with at most tm-1 binary AND/OR gates when input negations are free; if NOT gates are charged but shared, at most tm-1+m gates suffice.
proof: For each accepting input a, form the conjunction of its m literals, using m-1 binary AND gates (for m=1 this is one literal and uses zero). OR the t conjunctions using t-1 binary OR gates. The resulting DNF is true exactly on the accepting inputs. Its AND/OR cost is t(m-1)+(t-1)=tm-1. With charged NOT gates, negate each input variable that occurs negatively in any minterm once and share that output; there are at most m such variables, adding at most m gates.

gap: This identity does not bound the aggregate number of gates needed to eliminate arbitrary fan-in-2 circuits with unrestricted fan-out/sharing; the D7 aggregate inequality remains open.
proved_step: statement: For every n>=1, every A subseteq {0,1}^n, and every q in {0,...,n}, the average over uniformly chosen prefixes p in {0,1}^q of |{x in A: x_1...x_q=p}| equals |A|/2^q. Proof: sum_p sum_{x in A} 1[x begins with p] = sum_{x in A} 1 = |A|, since each x has exactly one length-q prefix; divide by 2^q.

gap: The collision identity does not control aggregate gate elimination for arbitrary fan-in-2 circuits with unrestricted sharing. A useful next obligation is to relate prefix collision counts of MCSP[m^c]'s accepting truth table to gate-elimination cost under a specified restriction process.
proved_step: statement: For every finite A subseteq {0,1}^n and q in {0,...,n}, if R_p=|{x in A:x_1...x_q=p}| for p in {0,1}^q, then 2^{-q} sum_p R_p^2 = 2^{-q}|{(x,y) in A^2: x_1...x_q=y_1...y_q}|. Proof: expand R_p^2 as sum over ordered pairs (x,y) in A^2 of the indicator that both have prefix p; summing over p counts the pair once if their prefixes agree and zero otherwise. Dividing by 2^q gives the identity. This expresses the second moment as a collision statistic and is sensitive to prefix clustering, unlike the first moment.

proved_step: statement: For integers K,B>=1 and 0<=t<=KB, among all integer vectors (R_1,...,R_K) with 0<=R_i<=B and sum_i R_i=t, the minimum of sum_i R_i^2 is (K-v)u^2+v(u+1)^2 where t=uK+v, 0<=v<K; the maximum is aB^2+r^2 where t=aB+r, 0<=r<B. Proof: for the minimum, if R_i>=R_j+2, replacing (R_i,R_j) by (R_i-1,R_j+1) changes the sum by -2(R_i-R_j)+2<0, so at a minimum all entries differ by at most one; the fixed sum forces v entries u+1 and K-v entries u. For the maximum, if 0<R_j<=R_i<B, moving one unit from j to i changes the sum by 2(R_i-R_j)+2>0; hence at a maximum at most one entry is strictly between 0 and B, and all others are 0 or B; the fixed sum forces a entries B, one entry r if r>0, and the rest 0. These vectors are feasible since t<=KB.

statement: For integers m>=1 and s>=0, the number of Boolean functions on m inputs computable by circuits with at most s ordered fan-in-2 gates over a basis of at most 16 Boolean operations is at most (m+s)(16(m+s)^2)^s (interpreting the s=0 case directly). Proof: Pad a circuit with unused gates to exactly s gates. In an ordered description, each gate chooses one of at most 16 operations and an ordered pair of predecessors among at most m+s available input or gate wires, giving at most 16(m+s)^2 choices. The output chooses one of at most m+s wires. Thus the number of descriptions is at most (m+s)(16(m+s)^2)^s, and each computes at most one Boolean function, so the number of distinct functions is no larger.

gap: This lemma does not establish a lower bound on the aggregate number of gates that become constant for restrictions of MCSP[m^c]. The remaining GE-3 obstacle is relating that statistic to the MCSP circuit's total size under arbitrary sharing.
proved_step: statement: Lemma (cofactor gate removal with free constants). For any fan-in-2 Boolean circuit C with s gates, any set I of input variables, and any assignment a in {0,1}^I, let E_a be the gates whose computed functions become constant after fixing I=a. Then C restricted by I=a has a fan-in-2 circuit of size at most s-|E_a|. Proof: traverse C in topological order, replace every gate in E_a by its constant value under the restriction, and feed that value to every consumer. Retain the other gates. The output is unchanged and each gate in E_a is removed once, including when it has multiple consumers. Consequently, for uniform a, E_a's average size is 2^{-|I|} sum_g |{a : gate g becomes constant under I=a}|.

gap: The counterexample shows that aggregate gate elimination cannot follow from circuit size alone: gates may compute functions independent of the fixed coordinates and survive every such restriction. A viable enriched lemma must condition on a structural relation between gate functions and restriction coordinates, then relate that statistic to MCSP[m^c] circuit size under arbitrary sharing.
refuted_approach: The proposed universal bound that every s-gate fan-in-2 circuit has at least s/2 gates constant on average after fixing one input is false. A one-gate circuit computing the other input has zero constant gates for both assignments of the fixed input; the finite search found this counterexample (cm-fa015cf1af5940fb).
evidence: DISCOVERY computation cm-fa015cf1af5940fb found the smallest two-input, one-gate counterexample: fixing x in a circuit whose sole gate computes y leaves that gate nonconstant for both x=0 and x=1. This matches the failure prediction that gates can avoid the fixed variable entirely.
proved_step: statement: Lemma (restriction-independent gates survive). Let C be a fan-in-2 Boolean circuit on variables X∪Y, and let g be a gate whose computed Boolean function depends only on Y. For every assignment a to X, the gate function after restricting X=a is the same function h(Y). If h is nonconstant, g remains nonconstant. Proof: write the gate function as h(Y). Substitution of a for X changes no argument of h, so the restricted gate still computes h(Y). Since h is nonconstant, it remains nonconstant for every a.

evidence: Elementary counting proof. This does not establish a lower bound on N in terms of MCSP prefix information, so its relation to the aggregate gate-elimination target remains limited.
proved_step: statement: Lemma (survival probability from one nonconstant cofactor). Let C be a fan-in-2 Boolean circuit with s gates on disjoint variable sets X∪Y, |X|=r. For each gate g and assignment a∈{0,1}^X, let g_a be its restricted Boolean function on Y. If N gates have at least one assignment a for which g_a is nonconstant, then under uniform a the expected number of nonconstant restricted gate functions is at least N/2^r. Proof: each counted gate has at least one surviving restriction among 2^r equally likely assignments, so its survival probability is at least 2^-r. The expected surviving-gate count is the sum of these indicator probabilities. No independence is required, and arbitrary fan-out does not affect the gate count.

statement: Lemma (survival of Y-only gates under X-restriction). Let C be a Boolean circuit on disjoint input sets X and Y, and let H be any set of gates whose computed functions are nonconstant and depend only on Y. For every assignment a to X, every gate in H computes the same nonconstant function of Y in C|_{X=a}; hence none is removed when replacing constant gates, and |C|−|E_a|≥|H|, where E_a is the set of gates that become constant after restriction. Proof: each gate g∈H computes h_g(Y) before restriction, with no dependence on X. Substituting X=a therefore leaves its function exactly h_g(Y). Since h_g is nonconstant, g is not in E_a. Thus H∩E_a=∅, so |E_a|≤|C|−|H| and the inequality follows. This holds pointwise for every a, even with arbitrary fan-out and shared gates.
proof: For each g in H, its Boolean function is h_g(Y), independent of X and nonconstant. Substituting any assignment a for X leaves h_g(Y) unchanged, so g does not become constant. Therefore H is disjoint from E_a and |E_a|≤|C|−|H|.

statement: Lemma (cofactor survival for Y-dependent gates). Let X,Y be disjoint Boolean input sets with |X|=q, and let f:{0,1}^X×{0,1}^Y->{0,1} depend on at least one Y input. For uniform a∈{0,1}^X, Pr[f(a,·) is nonconstant]≥2^{-q}. Proof: Y-dependence gives x*, y,y' with f(x*,y)≠f(x*,y'); hence the cofactor at x* is nonconstant, and a=x* has probability 2^{-q}. Sharpness: f(X,y)=1[X=x*]∧y has exactly one surviving cofactor. For any h such gate functions in a circuit, linearity of expectation gives expected at least h2^{-q} nonconstant gate cofactors, irrespective of shared fan-out.
proof: For each function choose a witnessing assignment x* and witnessing Y inputs y,y'. The random restriction equals x* with probability 2^{-q}, which preserves a nonconstant cofactor. Summing the survival indicators over gates and applying linearity of expectation gives the aggregate expectation; no independence is needed.

statement: Lemma (support-sensitive cofactor survival). Let C be a Boolean circuit on disjoint input sets X and Y, and for each gate g let f_g(X,Y) be its computed Boolean function. Let d_g be the number of coordinates of X on which f_g actually depends. If f_g depends on at least one coordinate of Y, then for a uniform a in {0,1}^X, Pr[f_g(a,·) is nonconstant] >= 2^{-d_g}. Consequently, for any set H of gates whose functions depend on Y, the expected number of gates in H with nonconstant cofactors is at least sum_{g in H} 2^{-d_g}.
proof: Fix g in H. Since f_g depends on Y, there are x*, y, y' with f_g(x*,y) != f_g(x*,y'). Fix the d_g coordinates in the X-support of f_g to their values in x*. For every assignment to the remaining X coordinates, the two evaluations still differ because f_g is independent of those coordinates. Thus at least a 2^{-d_g} fraction of all assignments to X give a nonconstant Y-cofactor. Summing the survival indicators over H and taking expectations proves the aggregate inequality by linearity of expectation; no independence between gates is needed. The bound is sharp: f(X,y)=1[X|_S=x*] AND y, where |S|=d, has a nonconstant cofactor on exactly one assignment to S.

statement: Sensitivity witness lemma. Let X,Y be finite nonempty sets and f:X×Y→{0,1}. For y0,y1∈Y, define D={x∈X:f(x,y0)≠f(x,y1)}. For each x∈X, call the restricted gate f(x,·) surviving if it is nonconstant on Y. Then at least |D| of the |X| restrictions survive. Proof: for every x∈D the two values f(x,y0),f(x,y1) differ, so f(x,·) takes both Boolean values and is nonconstant. Thus D is contained in the set of surviving restrictions, giving the cardinality inequality. In uniform form, survival probability is at least |D|/|X|.

statement: Averaged cofactor-survival bound. Let X,Y be finite nonempty sets and let f_1,...,f_s:X×Y→{0,1}. For each i,x let p_i(x)=|{y∈Y:f_i(x,y)=1}|/|Y|, and let S(x)=|{i:y↦f_i(x,y) is nonconstant}|. Then Σ_{x∈X}S(x) ≥ Σ_{x∈X}Σ_{i=1}^s 2p_i(x)(1-p_i(x)). Proof: choose independent uniform y0,y1∈Y. For each fixed x,i, the probability f_i(x,y0)≠f_i(x,y1) is p_i(x)(1-p_i(x))+(1-p_i(x))p_i(x)=2p_i(x)(1-p_i(x)). Whenever this disagreement occurs, the cofactor y↦f_i(x,y) is nonconstant. Thus pointwise the number of disagreeing (x,i) pairs is at most Σ_x S(x). Take expectation and use linearity of expectation to obtain the inequality.
